title: A Shared Calendar on the TV

slides.title: Intro
slides.transcript: [warmly] A Shared Calendar on the TV. <break time="0.4s" /> By Hisham Abu ella. <break time="0.8s" /> I wanted one calendar that my wife and I could both see: on both our phones, and on one screen in the house that shows the day without anyone opening anything. <break time="0.4s" /> I had the same rule as for texting my own A I: it lives on my own hardware, and only our own devices can reach it. So I asked Claude Code to build it, and a Raspberry Pi to put it on the TV. <break time="0.4s" /> Four pieces. The calendar: a small web app on the Mac, with Fast A P I and S Q Lite, and plain JavaScript, that installs on a phone like an app. Invites from email: meeting invites are picked up from Mail on the Mac, read only. Nothing is sent, moved or deleted. Shared links: one private link per person, with exactly what they may see and do. And the wall display: a Raspberry Pi on the TV that shows today and the next three days, full screen, all day.

slides.title: Two days
slides.transcript: Two Days, Twenty-Two Commits. <break time="0.5s" /> The first commit was the whole back end: events, repeat rules, sharing, email sync and tests. Then came review. A security reviewer agent read the code in several rounds, and every finding was fixed before the next one. By the end there were a hundred and forty-five tests, and a script that opens every screen at every size, in light and dark, and fails on low contrast, clipped text, or a button too small to tap. <break time="0.4s" /> Repeat rules took more care than I expected. Every Tuesday and Thursday until December fifteenth. The last Friday of the month. And the question every calendar has to ask when you change one meeting in a series: this event, this and following, or all events?

slides.title: Sharing
slides.transcript: Sharing It With My Wife. <break time="0.5s" /> Sharing works with links, one per person. Each link says what that person can do: see titles and places, or only busy; leave comments; block time of their own. A link can expire, and turning it off works at once. The link is shown one time when it is made, and the server keeps only a hash of it. <break time="0.4s" /> My wife uses a link that sees the full details. Time blocked through a shared link shows up on my calendar hatched, and labelled with the person's name, so a plan can be seen before it clashes. <break time="0.4s" /> A bug on the Home Screen. A shared link saved to a phone's Home Screen opened my sign-in page, instead of the shared calendar. The app had one manifest for everyone, and it said: start at the front page. Now each shared link, and the TV's link, gets its own, so the icon opens the calendar it was saved from.

slides.title: Invites
slides.transcript: Invites You Can Trust. <break time="0.5s" /> Every fifteen minutes the app asks Mail on the Mac for recent messages that look like invites, and reads their calendar parts. The interesting part is not reading them. It is deciding who is allowed to change an event by email, because the from line of an email is easy to fake. <break time="0.4s" /> So an invite only counts as coming from its sender when the email provider checked it on arrival, and the app reads that check only from the part of the headers the provider itself wrote. A change or a cancellation is accepted only from the person who sent the original invite. Anything it cannot confirm still appears, once, with a yellow note: check this invite.

slides.title: The TV
slides.transcript: The TV. <break time="0.5s" /> The display is its own page, made for a screen across the room. A large clock and the date. Today, with all-day items first, what is on now and what is next, finished events folded into one line, and plus two more, when the day is too full. Then the next three days. It refreshes every minute, stays dark, and never needs a touch. On a screen turned on its side it switches to a portrait layout by itself, and a few photos rotate on it between updates. <break time="0.4s" /> It opens with its own read-only link, so the TV can show the day, but can't change anything.

slides.title: The Pi
slides.transcript: The Raspberry Pi. <break time="0.5s" /> The Pi's whole job is to open one page and keep it open. That turned out to need a few steps. <break time="0.4s" /> One. It powers on and signs in by itself, so after a power cut the TV comes back to the calendar with nobody touching it. Two. It waits for the Mac. A small script checks the Wi-Fi, the private network, and the calendar's health page first, so the screen never opens on an error. Three. Chromium opens full screen, in kiosk mode: no bars, no pop-ups, no restore pages. Four. If it ever closes, it comes back. The script starts it again five seconds later. <break time="0.4s" /> The display link carries a secret, so it never appears in a script or a log. It lives in a file on the Pi that only its own user can read. To change it, I copy the new link on the Mac and run one command: it sends the clipboard to the Pi over S S H, and restarts the screen. <break time="0.4s" /> The bug that froze the whole Pi. The whole Pi froze. The system log said the S D card was stuck being busy. Chromium writes to its profile and cache all the time, and the card couldn't keep up. The fix was to give Chromium a profile and cache that live in memory instead, emptied at every boot. The card now has almost nothing to do. <break time="0.4s" /> One small one, too: the Pi's region is set to Britain, which means a twenty-four hour clock, so the link asks for a twelve hour clock itself.

slides.title: Private
slides.transcript: Keeping It Private. <break time="0.5s" /> Only our devices. The app listens only on the Mac itself. Our phones and the Pi reach it through Tailscale, my private network, and it is never published to the open internet. <break time="0.4s" /> Links, not passwords, for guests. Shared links are long random tokens, stored only as hashes, with their own limits on how often they can be tried. Sign out everywhere ends every session at once. <break time="0.4s" /> Nothing loaded from elsewhere. No fonts, scripts or styles from other sites. The page only runs what the Mac itself serves.

slides.title: AI and next
slides.transcript: My A I Can Use It Too. <break time="0.5s" /> The calendar has an M C P server, so Claude Code and my A I engine can list events, find free time on a day, add an event, or block time, the same way I would. Find me an hour on Thursday, is now a question, not a search. <break time="0.4s" /> [warmly] The best family calendar is the one you don't have to open. <break time="0.4s" /> What's next. A proper sign-in for my wife, instead of a link. Testing invites from real email providers, not only the ones the tests describe. And trying the drag to move gesture on a real iPad, which so far has only been tested in a browser. <break time="0.4s" /> The calendar, the Pi setup, and this article were built with Claude Code.
